newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK interest rates rise sends pound tumbling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK interest rates rise sends pound tumbling.

text.p: The Bank of England raised official interest rates on Thursday for the fourth month in a row and sent the pound tumbling by hinting that this would be the last policy tightening for some time.
The Bank's new Monetary Policy Committee, which was empowered by the Labour government in May to determine monetary policy, raised rates to 7.0 percent from 6.75 percent.
Although many economists had argued that the need for a fourth rate rise was finely balanced, the increase had been widely expected.

But the Bank's unusually forthright accompanying statement sent financial markets into a spin, with the pound falling nearly five pfennigs against the deutschemark at one point and London shares setting yet another record high.
The committee acknowledged that the strong pound was putting severe pressure on exporters, but said this was largely due to factors outside the influence of British policy-makers.

"In the light of the prospect for domestic demand and on the basis of all the evidence currently available, the committee judges that today's rise is necessary to put the economy on track for achieving the inflation target of 2.5 percent looking two years ahead," it said.

The clinching sentence, as far as financial markets were concerned, read: "Upward pressures on the exchange rate should be reduced by the perception that interest rates have reached a level consistent with the inflation target."
The pound slid to 2.9762/72 marks by early afternoon compared with around 3.0130 before the noon announcement, while the FTSE 100 index surged to a record 5094.7.
"The message is clear that that's it for now," said Ian Stewart, an economist at Merrill Lynch in London. "It is highly unlikely rates will go up again in September."
But Stewart and other City economists believe interest rates will have to rise again at some point.

"It is clear that domestic demand is strengthening, underpinned not just by windfall gains, but also by real income gains, a rising housing market, tight labour market and strong stock market," said Ciaran Barr, an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"Further base rate rises will be necessary to ensure that growth slows sufficiently."
Britain's gross domestic product grew an annual 3.4 percent in the second quarter, a level which most economists believe cannot be sustained for long without higher inflation.

The pound has risen as much as 25 percent against major currencies as international investors and speculators piled into the currency to take advantage of Britain's booming economy and rising interest rates.
While good news for Britons holidaying abroad, the strong pound has seriously hurt exporters whose goods become much more expensive in foreign currency terms.

Bank of England Governor Eddie George, who chairs the monetary policy committee, has expressed concern that rampant consumer spending will lead to a resurgence in inflation, which is at historically low levels in Britain.

But some economists argue that consumer spending growth is fuelled by one-off "windfall" gains totalling an estimated 35 billion pounds ($56 billion), which millions of Britons are receiving this year as mutually owned building societies turn themselves into banks. They believe the impact of the windfalls will largely disappear after this year.
Business organisations and trade unions were united in condemning the move.

"While robust consumer spending points to robust growth in the short term, there is increasing evidence that the weakness in the export sector will slow the pace of UK economic growth significantly during 1998," said Kate Barker, chief economic adviser to the Confederation of British Industry.
"Strong sterling means serious problems for many companies today. We are concerned that this will exacerbate these difficulties in the months to come."
The British Chambers of Commerce described the rate rise as a "body blow" to exporters while the Trades Union Congress (TUC) said the rate rise could put jobs at risk.
"The latest interest rate rise will put jobs at risk by keeping the pound high and slowing the economy next year," TUC deputy general secretary Brendan Barber said in a statement.

British government bond futures also soared after the rate rise. Commercial banks immediately raised their own base lending rates and Cheltenham & Gloucester took the lead in raising its variable mortgage rate to 8.45 percent from 8.2.
Most British home-owners have variable-rate home loans and could start to feel the pinch soon as their monthly repayments increase yet again.
($ = 0.624 British Pounds)
